etymology: Hebrew ’immer, perhaps “he hath said” or “lamb,” the head of the sixteenth of the four and twenty priestly courses appointed by David and Zadok.
biblical_def: Immer is named as the head of the sixteenth course of the priests, when David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, divided the sons of Aaron into four and twenty courses, that each might minister in the house of the LORD in its appointed season (1Ch 24:14). The lot fell to Immer in his place among his brethren, and his house was reckoned a course of the sanctuary for ever. The name endured, for the children of Immer are numbered among the priests who returned from the captivity of Babylon to serve again at the altar (Ezr 2:37), and Pashur the son of Immer, governor in the house of the LORD, is the priest who smote Jeremiah and put him in the stocks (Jer 20:1). The dictionary honours that the course of Immer kept its station through the centuries, from the ordering of David to the return from exile, a witness to the constancy of the LORD’s appointment. Yet the priesthood of Immer, like all the sons of Aaron, was hindered by death from continuing in office; many priests there were, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death. Immer stands therefore as a shadow pointing beyond itself to the great High Priest who hath an unchangeable priesthood, even the Lord Jesus, who ever liveth to make intercession, and whose course is not for a fortnight in the year but for ever.

biblical_def: Hezir is named as the head of the seventeenth course of the priests in the ordering which David and the chief of the fathers made for the sons of Aaron, that the house of the LORD might be served in a settled and equal course (1Ch 24:15). The lot fell to Hezir in his turn among his brethren, and his house was reckoned a division of the sanctuary. A man of the same name is found among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah, when the people bound themselves with an oath to walk in God’s law and to forsake the strange wives and the profaning of the sabbath (Neh 10:20); whether the priestly course endured in that sealing or another Hezir is meant, the name witnesses to households given to the service and covenant of the LORD. The dictionary does not labour to multiply what Scripture leaves brief; it honours that the Spirit of God set down even the seventeenth course by name, that the order of His house might be known. The priests of Aaron served by course, each in his fortnight, hindered by death from continuing and needing ever to be renewed. Hezir stands therefore as a shadow of the better priesthood, for our Lord, of whom Moses spake nothing concerning that office, hath by Himself purged our sins and abideth a priest continually. The seventeenth course passed, but the great High Priest passeth not away.

etymology: Hebrew pethachyah, “the LORD hath opened” or “whom the LORD sets free,” the head of the nineteenth priestly course, and a Levite who led in confession.
biblical_def: Pethahiah is named as the head of the nineteenth course of the priests in the division which David appointed for the sons of Aaron, that the house of the LORD might be served in order (1Ch 24:16). His name signifies “the LORD hath opened,” a fitting word for one set to minister where the way into the holy place was opened by sacrifice. The same name is borne by a Levite who stood among those that led the great congregation in confession and worship after the return, when the Levites said, Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever (Neh 9:5), and by a man of the children of Zerah of Judah who was at the king’s hand in all matters concerning the people (Neh 11:24). The dictionary honours that the name, meaning the LORD’s opening, is found both at the altar and in the mouth of those who called Israel to bless their God. The courses of Aaron, opened to their service by lot and by birth, ministered in turn and passed away, hindered by death; but the LORD hath opened by His Son a new and living way into the holiest, which the blood of bulls and goats could never open. Pethahiah stands as a witness that He who opened the priestly courses hath now opened heaven itself, that we may come boldly to the throne of grace through the great High Priest who ever liveth.

biblical_def: Jehezekel is named as the head of the twentieth course of the priests in the ordering which David made for the sons of Aaron, casting lots that each course might minister in the house of the LORD in its season (1Ch 24:16). His name signifies “God will strengthen,” the very name borne in its fuller form by the prophet Ezekiel, who was himself a priest carried to Babylon and made a watchman to the house of Israel. Of this Jehezekel of the twentieth course the Scripture records nothing beyond his name and his place; he is a head of a division, otherwise unknown, set down by the Spirit of God in the careful reckoning of the priesthood. The dictionary does not feign a history where the LORD was pleased to leave silence; it honours that even the twentieth course was named, that the order of God’s house might stand complete. There is strength in the name for the weary servant, for the priest could not minister in his own might but only as God should strengthen him. The courses of Aaron were renewed because the priests died; but the strength of the new covenant is the great High Priest who is alive for evermore and was raised by the power of an endless life. Jehezekel stands as a witness that the God who strengthened His priests of old now strengthens His people through the One who ever liveth, that they faint not but serve Him in their appointed course.

etymology: Hebrew yakin, “he will establish” or “whom God establishes,” the head of the twenty-first of the four and twenty priestly courses; to be distinguished from Jachin the pillar of the temple porch.
biblical_def: Jachin is named as the head of the twenty-first course of the priests in the division which David appointed for the sons of Aaron (1Ch 24:17), and the priests of his course are reckoned among those who dwelt at Jerusalem after the return from captivity (Neh 11:10). He is to be distinguished from Jachin the right-hand pillar of brass which Solomon set up in the porch of the temple, though both names spring from the same root and both speak of establishment, for the pillar Jachin signified that the LORD would establish His house. The man Jachin, head of a priestly course, bears in his very name the promise that God will establish; and his house, kept through the centuries and restored after the exile, is itself a token of that establishing. The dictionary honours that the Spirit of God set down this course by name, that the order of the priesthood might be known and the LORD’s faithfulness remembered. The courses of Aaron, though established for a season, were shaken by death and exile, and could not stand of themselves; yet the LORD established a Priest after the order of Melchisedec, whom He hath sworn and will not repent, a priest for ever. Jachin stands therefore as a witness that the establishing of God’s house rests not upon the changing courses of men but upon the unchangeable oath of the LORD, who hath set His Son a Priest for ever, that His sanctuary may not be moved.

etymology: Hebrew gamul, “weaned” or “rewarded, recompensed,” the head of the twenty-second of the four and twenty priestly courses appointed by David.
biblical_def: Gamul is named as the head of the twenty-second course of the priests in the division which David, with Zadok and the chief of the fathers, appointed for the sons of Aaron (1Ch 24:17). The lot fell to Gamul in his order, and his house was reckoned a course of the house of the LORD, to minister in its appointed turn. His name signifies “weaned” or “rewarded,” from a root that speaks both of the child weaned from the breast and of the recompense the LORD deals to His servants. Of Gamul himself the Scripture records nothing beyond his name and his place; he is a head of a course, otherwise unknown, yet written by the Spirit of God in the careful order of the priesthood. The dictionary does not invent a history where the LORD was pleased to leave silence; it honours that the twenty-second course was named, that none might be wanting in the reckoning of God’s house. There is teaching in the name, for as a child must be weaned to grow, so the servant of God must be weaned from the world to serve at the altar; and the LORD rewardeth them that diligently seek Him. The courses of Aaron served and were recompensed in their day, yet looked for a better reward. Gamul stands as a witness that the great High Priest will render to every faithful servant the recompence of the reward, even an inheritance that fadeth not away.

etymology: Hebrew delayah, “the LORD hath delivered” or “whom the LORD draweth up,” the head of the twenty-third of the four and twenty priestly courses appointed by David.
biblical_def: Delaiah is named as the head of the twenty-third course of the priests in the division which David appointed for the sons of Aaron, that each course might serve the house of the LORD in its season (1Ch 24:18). His name signifies “the LORD hath delivered,” or, as some render it, “whom the LORD draweth up,” as one drawn up out of deep waters. Of this Delaiah of the twenty-third course the Scripture records nothing beyond his name and his place; others of the name appear in the line of the kings and among the returned exiles, yet the priestly course bears the name as a standing confession of the LORD’s delivering. The dictionary does not feign a history where God was pleased to leave silence; it honours that the twenty-third course was named, that the order of His house might stand complete. There is a gospel in the name, for the priest ministered at the altar of a delivering God, where the blood of sacrifice spake of deliverance from the curse. The courses of Aaron themselves needed deliverance, being hindered by death and unable to save themselves; but the great High Priest is able to save to the uttermost that come unto God by Him. Delaiah stands as a witness that the LORD who delivered His people of old hath wrought a greater deliverance by His Son, and that His name is rightly upon them who serve the God of all deliverance.

etymology: Hebrew ma‘azyahu, “the LORD is a refuge” or “consolation of the LORD,” the head of the twenty-fourth and last priestly course, and a sealer of the covenant.
biblical_def: Maaziah is named as the head of the four and twentieth course of the priests, the last in the division which David appointed for the sons of Aaron, that the whole house of God might be served in an orderly round (1Ch 24:18). His name signifies “the LORD is a refuge,” or “consolation of the LORD,” a fitting word to close the order of the priesthood, for the altar at which they ministered was the place of refuge for the guilty seeking mercy. A priest named Maaziah is found among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah, when the people set their hand to walk in God’s law and to keep His commandments (Neh 10:8), so that the name of the last course is bound up with the renewing of covenant faithfulness. The dictionary honours that the twenty-fourth course completed the round, that no part of the LORD’s service was left unprovided. The courses of Aaron, four and twenty in number, served and were renewed and at last gave place; for the LORD is a refuge not in the changing rounds of dying priests but in the one Priest who abideth ever. Maaziah, last of the courses, stands as a witness that the whole shadow of the Aaronic order pointed to its consummation in Christ, who is the true refuge of His people, the consolation of Israel, and the High Priest whose ministry shall never be succeeded nor superseded, world without end.

corruption_paragraphs: Maaziah, last of the priestly courses, is a name of the sacred record, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name closing the four and twenty courses may know it for a real house in a real order, set by a real God to minister at His altar in its season.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD Himself is the refuge to which all the rounds of His house point. He who set Maaziah as the last course, and whose name confessed Him a refuge, hath made the Son a High Priest consecrated for evermore. The saint in trouble may flee to that refuge, for the whole shadow of Aaron’s order is fulfilled in Christ, the consolation of His people and the very present help in trouble.

etymology: Hebrew charim, “consecrated” or “dedicated to God,” the head of the third of the four and twenty priestly courses; to be distinguished from the returnee house and town of Harim.
biblical_def: Harim is named as the head of the third course of the priests in the division which David made for the sons of Aaron, when the lot came forth in its order (1Ch 24:8). His name signifies “consecrated” or “dedicated to God,” a most fitting name for one set apart to minister in holy things. He is to be distinguished from the house and place of Harim among the returnees, for the children of Harim are reckoned both among the priests and among the people who came up out of Babylon (Ezr 2:39), and Malchijah the son of Harim is named as one who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Neh 3:11). The dictionary honours that the priestly course of Harim, consecrated to the LORD, endured from the ordering of David through the exile and the return, a witness to the keeping of a name set apart unto God. The courses of Aaron were all consecrated, sanctified to their office by anointing and by blood; yet their consecration could not perfect them, being made priests after the law of a carnal commandment. Harim, the consecrated, stands therefore as a shadow of the true Consecrated One, the Son who is consecrated for evermore by the word of the oath. The dignity of being set apart unto God is fulfilled in Christ, and through Him in His people, who are a holy priesthood to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God.

corruption_paragraphs: Harim the priest is a name of the sacred record, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine it. The dictionary records it that the reader who meets the name among the four and twenty courses may know it for a real house in a real order, distinct from the town and returnee house of like name, set apart by a real God to His holy service.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is consecration, the setting apart of a servant wholly unto God. He who named Harim, the consecrated, in the third course is the same who hath made the Son consecrated for evermore by the word of the oath. The saint may remember that he too is built a lively stone into a holy priesthood, set apart to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
